comparison: Both strongly support the identification and characterization of ELYSAs (C3-C5, C32-C36). OpenEval provides detailed evidence from immunofluorescence, quantitative analysis, and electron microscopy. Peer reviewers affirm these findings as 'convincing' and 'well-conducted' with all three reviewers accepting the structural characterization.

Both support the temporal dynamics of ELYSA formation and disassembly (C37-C38, C42-C43, C49). OpenEval cites comprehensive quantitative 3D analysis from Figure 2. Peer reviewers accept the dynamics during maturation and post-fertilization disassembly as convincing. OpenEval covers additional quantitative details (C40-C41, C46-C48, C51-C52) not explicitly mentioned in peer review.

Partial overlap on spatial dynamics (C51-C52). OpenEval R2 includes peripheral localization in MII stage as part of comprehensive temporal analysis. Peer R12 specifically highlights the redistribution from cytoplasmic to cortical localization, accepting these spatial dynamics.

Both support the ultrastructural characterization (C56-C60). OpenEval emphasizes CLEM data showing detailed ultrastructure with quantitative measurements. Peer reviewers accept the structural contents including endosomes, lysosomes, and autophagic structures. OpenEval includes additional technical details (C53-C55, C94) about correlative microscopy methods.

Both support LC3 localization to ELYSAs (C6, C61-C63). OpenEval provides detailed evidence from immunofluorescence and quantitative analysis. Peer reviewers accept the presence of autophagic components. OpenEval covers additional quantitative changes during maturation (C64-C67) that peer R4 does not explicitly address.

Minor overlap on LC3 dynamics during maturation (C64-C65). OpenEval R4 documents quantitative changes in LC3 positivity. Peer R12 accepts spatial and size dynamics during maturation, providing complementary validation of developmental changes.

Both support actin-dependent ELYSA dynamics (C73-C75, C100). OpenEval provides detailed cytoskeletal inhibitor experiments distinguishing actin from tubulin effects. Peer reviewers explicitly accept that ELYSAs migrate to periphery 'in an actin-dependent manner.' Both evaluations align on the specificity of actin involvement.

Both support V1-subunit localization dynamics (C8, C77). OpenEval cites live-cell imaging showing peripheral V1A-mCherry localization. Peer reviewers accept V1-subunit recruitment during ELYSA disassembly and its role in lysosomal acidification. Peer R6 also addresses post-disassembly effects (C87, C111) covered in OpenEval R7 and R14.

Both address ELYSA assembly mechanisms (C76). OpenEval R6 documents assembly through live-cell imaging. Peer R13 accepts the assembly dynamics as part of the convincing localization and dynamics data. Agreement on the observational findings regarding assembly.

Both support differential acidification of ELYSAs (C79-C81, C86). OpenEval provides detailed evidence from LysoSensor/LysoTracker differential staining with ratiometric analysis. Peer reviewers accept that endolysosomal compartments in oocytes are 'less acidic and therefore non-degradative' with pH decreasing post-fertilization.

Both support post-fertilization acidification mechanism (C9-C10, C88-C89). OpenEval documents increased V1A localization and LysoSensor-positive structures after disassembly. Peer reviewers accept that V1-subunit targeting increases acidity in embryos post-fertilization. Strong agreement on the mechanistic interpretation.

Both support proteolytic activity findings (C90-C91). OpenEval cites Magic Red cathepsin B staining showing activity in ELYSAs but lower than isolated lysosomes. Peer reviewers accept that ELYSAs prevent lysosomes from being activated and facilitate proteolysis after fertilization. Complete agreement on lower proteolytic activity in ELYSAs.

Both support the main functional interpretation (C11, C92, C112). OpenEval finds the 'static state' interpretation well-supported by collective evidence, though notes 'static' may be somewhat overstated. Peer reviewers describe findings as 'important' and 'well-conducted' with the model 'supported by experimental evidence.' Both accept the functional significance.

Both support the relationship between ELYSAs and ELVAs (C7, C104-C106). OpenEval finds the comparison reasonable and the conclusion that they are likely identical structures is a reasonable inference. Peer reviewers explicitly state ELYSAs are 'most likely the same' as ELVAs and note the studies are complementary. Strong agreement on structural identity.

Both address background claims (C1-C2). OpenEval finds these supported by appropriate citations to established literature. Peer reviewers do not challenge these concepts and implicitly accept the background framework. Agreement on contextual foundation.

Both address V1-subunit localization summary (C111). OpenEval R14 finds this summary statement well-supported by imaging data. Peer R6 accepts V1-subunit dynamics and its role in increasing lysosomal acidity. Agreement on this key finding.

OpenEval R12 addresses additional detailed observations (C39, C44-C45, C50, C68) from quantitative analysis that are not explicitly discussed in peer review results. These include specific measurements and developmental stage comparisons that peer reviewers did not separately evaluate.

OpenEval R13 identifies speculative claims and research gaps (C95-C98, C103, C119) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are appropriate for Discussion but lack direct experimental support. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these speculative elements, focusing instead on experimentally supported findings.
